title: 8 Reasons I Embrace Arguments in my Classroom
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart Jr. lists eight reasons he built an argumentative culture into his English and world history classes, prompted by former students saying they would miss the intense arguments. His central claim is that arguments, done well, are cooperative rather than adversarial and work as a tool of classroom community and character formation. He ties them to collaboration, higher-order thinking, civility and humility, a unifying view of academia, democratic habits and career self-advocacy. The closing reason is a small experiment: when he finally let students vote on a debate winner, it produced hurt feelings the unscored debates never did. The lesson is that the value lies in the practice and shared search for truth, not in a winner.
points: Argument pulls in even reticent students because it demands collaboration over a substantive text or topic.
Done right, argument builds community, since it is a shared effort to get to the bottom of things rather than a contest.
Students themselves learned that respectful arguers who concede valid points are more persuasive, making argument a character-building routine.
Argument as an organizing frame (Graff) makes school feel more coherent and prepares students to advocate for themselves in work and civic life.
Declaring debate winners backfired, showing that unscored debates keep the focus on cooperation.
quotes: Arguments beg for collaboration. Whether in pairs, in triads, in teams, or as a whole class, when students are engaged with a substantive text or topic, even the most reticent ones tend to get involved.

But arguments are more than competitive when we do them right; in fact, they’re downright cooperative. Arguments are about “getting to the bottom of things,” to borrow from Williams and McEnerney (as quoted in CCSS Appendix A). They are an expression of our classroom desire to get to the truth.

For my students to flourish in college or a career, I know they’ll need more than academic skills; they’ll need character. The great thing about arguments is that they can build some really valuable character strengths.

During this past school year, I remember when students began vocalizing on their own that respectful arguers were more powerful than disrespectful arguers, and that arguers who were willing to concede a point were more convincing than those who stubbornly (and often stupidly) ignored any validity in an opposing claim.
Teaching students about this culture and helping them see it is a key way of making school more cohesive and sensible to them.

I want my students to be able to advocate for themselves; in a competitive job market, this is going to be crucial. If my kids can’t show why they are a great candidate, and if they can’t analyze their job search and create a winning strategy, they’ll have a hard time getting a job.

The moral of the story is simply that my in-class debates didn’t need a winner because, at the end of them, we all had practiced the items on the list above, and at debate’s end, we had all cooperated in getting closer to “the bottom of things.
